block.heading: Supply elasticity on a diagram
block.text:
Supply works the same way. Two workshops each make 50 chairs a month at N$400. The price rises 50 per cent, to N$600. Workshop A, with unused machines, raises output 80 per cent, to 90 chairs: PES is 1.6, elastic. Workshop B, near capacity, reaches 60 chairs, 20 per cent more: PES is 0.4, inelastic.

![Supply elasticity diagram](diagrams/item-6145-3.3-020-proc-answer.png)

A vertical supply curve is perfectly inelastic (PES 0), a horizontal one perfectly elastic, and a straight supply line through the origin unit elastic (PES 1) at every point.

item.prompt: Two furniture workshops each supply 50 chairs a month at N$400 a chair. The price rises to N$600. Workshop A, which has unused machines, increases supply to 90 chairs a month; workshop B, already near capacity, increases supply to 60 chairs a month. Assume straight supply lines and unchanged other supply conditions. Use these data to draw both supply curves on the same axes, with price on the vertical axis. Show the change for each workshop and label each curve with its price elasticity of supply (PES), calculated from the initial values (4).
item.canonical_answer: Draw both supply curves through the original point R (50, N$400) on the same labelled axes: price (N$ per chair) vertically, quantity supplied (chairs per month) horizontally. Workshop A's curve also passes through (90, N$600) and workshop B's through (60, N$600); an arrow along each curve shows the movement from R as price rises. Price rises by 50 per cent. Workshop A: +80% ÷ 50% = 1.6, so supply is elastic (above 1): its unused machines let it expand output quickly. Workshop B: +20% ÷ 50% = 0.4, so supply is inelastic (below 1): near capacity it can add little output in the short term. Because both curves share the same axes and starting point, workshop A's flatter curve is the more elastic one over this change.

Change: movement along each curve from that point to (90, N$600) for workshop A and to (60, N$600) for workshop B (1).
